items.prompt: Define whole-text structure, and state the task it is set on.
items.canonical_answer: Whole-text structure means the shape of a piece from its opening to its ending: what it promises, how it develops, and how it closes. It is set on the extended writing task — one continuous piece of 600–900 words in one of three categories, worth twenty-five marks — where the shape is planned before the writing and earned by it.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the shape from opening to ending, promised, developed and closed.
The task’s terms — 600–900 words, three categories, twenty-five marks — are part of the definition’s frame.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What shape does each of the three Section B categories tend to take?
items.canonical_answer: A story takes an arc: situation, conflict, turning point, resolution that shows the change. A discursive piece takes an exploration: the question opened, the sides given room, a reasoned view reached. A review takes a judgement: what is reviewed introduced, the criteria set, the evidence weighed, the verdict landed. The plan starts from the category’s own shape, because each is what its reader arrives expecting.
marking_guidance: Credit the three shapes: the arc, the exploration, the judgement, each with its stages.
The features are what the plan begins from, so an answer with one shape has a third of the card.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the steps for planning a 600–900-word piece.
items.canonical_answer: First fix the purpose and the audience, because the shape serves them. Second choose the shape: the arc, the exploration, the judgement, or the shape the task suggests. Third mark the sections: what each does, in order, and where the turning point or verdict sits. Fourth give each section its share of the words — roughly 100 to open, 400 to 600 across the middle, 100 to end, so the ending keeps its room.
marking_guidance: Credit the four steps in order: purpose and audience, shape, sections, word shares.
The shares are what make the plan a budget rather than a wish.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between chronological and thematic organisation, and how is the choice made?
items.canonical_answer: Chronological organisation follows time’s order — first this, then that — and thematic organisation follows the argument’s or picture’s own logic: the cheapest objection first, the widest view last, the senses in a visitor’s order. The choice is made for effect, not from habit: a day’s memoir wants time’s shape because the day is the story; a review wants themes because the deciding reader wants teaching, value, verdict — and the test is which order serves the purpose the piece is for.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: time’s order against the argument’s or picture’s own order.
Must give the test: the choice is for effect against purpose — chronology kept or broken for a reason.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A story opens with the narrator finding an unopened letter, and the letter’s contents are only revealed in the final paragraph. How does holding the outcome back work on the reader?
items.canonical_answer: Holding the outcome back keeps the reader reading because the question stays open: "what is in the letter" is planted in the first paragraph and every page between is read partly to close it, and the reader’s guesses do the holding work — each guess is a small investment in the answer. The delayed answer lands harder for the wait: it arrives into a reader who has imagined three versions of it, and whatever it is, the reader feels the gap between guess and truth, which is the mechanism — the withheld thing is a debt the ending repays with interest.
marking_guidance: Must name the mechanism in the story’s own words: the question held open, the guesses as investment.
Must trace the effect: the answer lands harder for the wait, because the reader has imagined versions of it.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: An article argues for later school starts, and after its main point it gives a paragraph to the bus-schedule objection — and answers it in the same paragraph. How does placing the counterargument there strengthen the piece?
items.canonical_answer: Placing the counterargument beside the point, and answering it there, strengthens the piece because the reader meets the objection while the case is strong enough to beat it: the objection is voiced honestly, so the reader who was raising it feels heard, and the answer follows before the doubt can harden. The reader also watches the argument survive its strongest test, which does more for its authority than another supporting point would — the counterargument is a weight the piece lifts to show it can.
marking_guidance: Must name the mechanism at the level of the words: the objection voiced and answered while the case is strong.
Must trace the effect on the reader: the doubt feels heard, and the argument’s authority grows from surviving the test.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A description of a market ends, not on a summary of the place, but on one image: the fruit seller stacking her last pyramid in the fading light. How does ending on one image work on the reader?
items.canonical_answer: Ending on one image makes the piece memorable because memory keeps the last thing given: the whole market — its noise, its smells, its people — has been distilled into one picture that the reader carries out, and the image does the summarising without a summary’s flatness. The fading light adds a closing charge: the market’s day is ending with the piece, and the reader feels the place stop rather than the writing stop, which is the difference between an ending and a stop.
marking_guidance: Must name the mechanism in the image’s words: the last thing given is what memory keeps.
Must trace the effect: the place stops with the piece rather than the writing merely finishing.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between an ending and a stop, and how is the test applied to a draft?
items.canonical_answer: An ending resolves what the piece opened: it answers the question the opening raised, completes the image it planted, or lands the argument it built. A stop merely finishes: the words run out or the clock does, and the reader is dropped where the piece should have landed them. The test on a draft is the return: read the first paragraph, then the last, and ask whether the last one answers, completes or lands the first — if the two could belong to different pieces, the piece stopped.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: resolution of what was opened against mere finishing.
Must give the test: first and last paragraphs read together — an ending answers the opening, a stop leaves it.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A draft’s final paragraph runs: "So that is my view. There are other views but I have given mine. The end." What has gone wrong, and what would fix it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is the rushed ending: the resolution is compressed into a formula, no question is answered and no image completed, and the reader is dropped rather than landed. The fix is to give the ending its planned room: return to the opening’s question or image — the one the piece spent 500 words raising — and resolve it in a paragraph that earns its place, which is what the last 100 words of the word-share were kept for.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the rushed, formulaic ending that resolves nothing.
Must give the fix: the ending’s room kept, the opening returned to and resolved.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the steps for sharing 600–900 words across a plan.
items.canonical_answer: First, total the words the task allows and set the ending’s 100 aside before anything else, because the ending is the section that gets spent by accident. Second, give the opening about 100: enough to establish and promise, not enough to answer. Third, divide the remaining 400 to 700 across the developing sections by the job each does — the section with the turning point gets the room it needs. Fourth, check the plan against the range: if the sections do not fill 600, they are too thin to develop.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps in order: total, reserve the ending, divide the middle, check the range.
The ending’s reservation first is the habit the steps exist to teach.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Why does the 600–900-word range have a lower limit at all?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that development needs room: 600 words is where developed sections become possible — where a point can be claimed, reasoned, exemplified and carried, two or three times over — and anything much shorter thins every section alike. The range is not a formality: it is the space the task’s own rewards require, because the table rewards ideas developed, and development is the first casualty of a thin piece.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: development needs room, and the limit marks where it becomes possible.
An answer about "looking serious" has described the impression, not the mechanism.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner finishes Section A in seventy minutes and writes 430 words for the 600–900-word task. What has gone wrong, and how is it prevented?
items.canonical_answer: What has gone wrong is the piece written well short of the range, and the cause is usually the one named — Section A took too long — so the extended piece was started late and thinned to fit. The sections shrink, the development goes first, and the ending goes second, and the mark reads the task as only partly done. The prevention is time discipline set before the exam: Section A carries its own marks and no more, and a fixed handover time — written on the plan — keeps Section B’s 600 words possible, because the range is part of the task it protects.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the piece written short, and the cause — Section A overrunning.
Must give the prevention: the fixed handover time, set before the exam, so the range stays possible.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is a topic sentence, and what does it do for a reader?
items.canonical_answer: A topic sentence states what a paragraph is about — usually its first sentence — and the reader uses it to know what they are reading and why. It is the paragraph’s door marked: the strongest ones make a claim the paragraph then carries, rather than announcing a subject and merely visiting it.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the sentence, usually first, that states the paragraph’s subject or claim.
What it does for the reader — orientation and expectation — is the definition’s purpose.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What do connectives and discourse markers do, with an example of each relation they carry?
items.canonical_answer: They show the relation between paragraphs and sentences so the reader does not have to guess it. Addition: "furthermore" adds a second reason. Contrast: "however" turns the argument. Sequence: "by then" places an event in the order. Consequence: "for this reason" hands the result over. The relation is the meaning they carry, which is why a piece without them asks its reader to supply its structure.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the visible relations between sentences and paragraphs, with examples.
The four relations — addition, contrast, sequence, consequence — are the working set the answer should name.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is internal coherence, and what does it rule out?
items.canonical_answer: Internal coherence means every sentence in a paragraph serves its topic: nothing belongs there that the topic sentence did not promise, and nothing the topic promised is missing. It rules out the paragraph that drifts — opening on the market’s noise and closing on the writer’s aunt — because the drift leaves the reader holding two paragraphs’ worth of material in one, unsure which one they were reading.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: every sentence serving the paragraph’s stated topic.
The two failures it rules out — the uninvited sentence and the broken promise — give the definition teeth.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a paragraph without its topic sentence: "By nine the queue reached the corner. Two men argued about places. A woman sold tea to the queue from a thermos. Nobody had tickets yet, but nobody left." Write a topic sentence for it.
items.canonical_answer: A model topic sentence: "The hour before the gates opened belonged to the queue, and the queue made its own entertainment." (Any sentence that names what the four details share — the queue’s life while waiting — and makes a claim the details then prove, does the job; the strongest versions do not merely label the subject but take a position on it.)
marking_guidance: Credit the topic sentence written for the text of the paragraph, because the fit is the skill.
The strongest answers make a claim rather than announce a subject, so the paragraph proves its sentence.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here are three sentences on one point: "The new bridge is beautiful. It was opened in March. Many people use it." Join them into one coherent paragraph with discourse markers.
items.canonical_answer: A model paragraph: "The new bridge is beautiful — opened in March, it already carries the town’s mornings, and its use is the point: a bridge can be lovely, but one that people choose over the old road has done its work." (Any version that shows the relations between the three facts — the opening date as context, the use as consequence of the beauty’s usefulness — rather than laying them side by side, meets the task; the markers do the joining, and the paragraph makes the three facts one point.)
marking_guidance: Credit the paragraph: the text of the three sentences joined with their relations visible, because the joining is the skill.
The strongest answers show consequence rather than just sequence, so the paragraph carries a point and not a list.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner’s 800-word piece has three paragraphs: one of 500 words, one of 200, one of 100. What is wrong with this paragraphing, and what is the rule?
items.canonical_answer: The error is paragraphing that hides the structure: a 500-word paragraph is five or six sections wearing one indent, and the reader cannot see where the piece turns — the 100-word tail is almost certainly a rushed ending squeezed into whatever room was left. The rule is that a new paragraph begins where a new job begins: the plan’s sections become the piece’s paragraphs (or pairs of them), and the breaks fall where the plan turns, so the shape planned on paper is the shape the reader meets on the page.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: paragraphs that do not match the piece’s jobs, hiding its structure.
Must give the rule: a new paragraph where a new job begins, so the plan becomes visible.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define development as it applies to a point or a moment in extended writing.
items.canonical_answer: Development is the detail, example or explanation that carries a point or a moment further: the claim plus its reason, the image plus its texture, the moment plus what it meant. It is what the table rewards as ideas developed — and it is the difference between a piece that names six things and a piece that carries three of them somewhere.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the detail, example or explanation that carries a point further.
The named pairs — claim and reason, image and texture, moment and meaning — are the definition’s examples.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the four moves for developing a point, in order.
items.canonical_answer: First the claim: state the point. Second the reason: say why it is so. Third the example: show it being so, with a real one small enough to see. Fourth the consequence: say what follows from it being so — what the reader should now think, feel or do. Four moves, and the point has been carried rather than named.
marking_guidance: Credit the four steps in order: claim, reason, example, consequence.
The order matters because each move gives the next its material.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a bare sentence: "The drought changed the town." Develop it into three sentences, using the four moves.
items.canonical_answer: A model development: "The drought changed the town — not dramatically, but in the small ways that add up: the church tank was padlocked in June, a thing nobody living had seen, and the queue at the borehole started forming in the dark. That was the change nobody could argue with: the town that had never thought about water now thought about it first." (Any three sentences that give the claim a reason, an example small enough to see, and a consequence do the job; the moves may be compressed but all four should be findable.)
marking_guidance: Credit the three sentences written from the text of the bare one, because the developing is the skill.
The strongest answers contain a visible example — the padlocked tank — and a consequence the reader can feel.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between developing a point and repeating it, and what is the test?
items.canonical_answer: Development adds reason, example or consequence; repetition adds only phrasing. "The market is busy. The market is full of people. The place is crowded" says one thing three times; "The market is busy — by nine you cannot cross the fruit row in a straight line" says it once and shows it. The test is the addition: what did the new sentence add? If the answer is only new words for the same content, it is repetition — and the piece is thinner than its word count claims.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: added reason, example or consequence against added phrasing only.
Must give the test: what did the second sentence add — content or only words?
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Plan a Section B-style narrative task of 600–900 words: the story must begin with a given sentence about a locked door, and create suspense throughout. Set out the shape, the sections with their word shares, the effect each section is for, and the ending. The model plan is the answer.
items.canonical_answer:
Shape: a story arc — situation, complication, turning point, resolution — for the task’s given opening sentence and its focus on suspense.
Sections and shares (830 words total):
1. Opening — 120 words. The given sentence starts the piece; establish the situation it implies and plant the question the suspense hangs on. Effect: the reader is placed and made curious in one breath.
2. Complication — 250 words. The ordinary begins to misbehave: three small wrongs, each slightly less explainable than the last. Effect: unease built by accumulation, the reader counting the wrongs.
3. Turning point — 250 words. The narrator learns what the wrongs were (the withheld information released at last). Effect: the question planted in section 1 is answered here and only here.
4. Fall and resolution — 150 words. The consequence plays out and is survived; the last image closes what the opening planted. Effect: relief, and the sense of an ending rather than a stop.
5. Ending — 60 words. One image, returning to the opening’s setting with the change visible in it. Effect: the piece’s parting gift — memorable because the last thing given is a picture.
Structure notes: hold the withheld information until section 3 — the question stays open, which is the suspense; mark the turning point with the piece’s only one-sentence paragraph; end on the image, not a summary.
marking_guidance: Credit the shape: the category’s own form — arc, exploration or judgement — made visible in the sections.
Credit the sections with their word shares, so the plan is a budget and the ending keeps its room.
Credit the effect each section is named for, and the ending that resolves what the opening raised — the plan’s words should show the structure, purpose and effect the piece is for.
The model plan is the standard: four steps, sections marked, shares given, ending kept.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Plan a Section B-style discursive task of 600–900 words: a magazine article exploring whether social media has made friendships stronger or weaker, giving both sides their strongest case. Set out the shape, the sections with their word shares, the effect each section is for, and the ending. The model plan is the answer.
items.canonical_answer:
Shape: a dialectical exploration — thesis, antithesis, synthesis — for a magazine article exploring whether social media has made friendships stronger or weaker.
Sections and shares (800 words total):
1. Opening — 100 words. The question opened honestly, with a small personal anchor. Effect: the reader is recruited as a juror, not a partisan.
2. The weaker case — 220 words. The best version of the argument that friendships have thinned: the phrase-talk, the unreachable friend, the group chat that replaces the visit. Two developed examples, both specific. Effect: the reader who holds this view feels heard, and the reader who does not feels its weight.
3. The stronger case — 220 words. The best version of the counterargument: the friend found again after twenty years, the group that organised a funeral in three days, the distance-collapsed Tuesday call. Two developed examples. Effect: the scales visibly move.
4. Synthesis — 180 words. The reasoned view: the tool changed the currency of friendship, not its worth — contact got cheaper and presence got rarer, and the friendships that matter are learning to spend both. Effect: the reader is given a position worth holding, earned from both sides.
5. Ending — 80 words. One image or anecdote that embodies the synthesis. Effect: memorable, and the resolution of the question the opening raised.
Structure notes: each case’s paragraph holds its examples and its counterargument-answer together; end on the image, not a summary of the synthesis.
marking_guidance: Credit the shape: the category’s own form — arc, exploration or judgement — made visible in the sections.
Credit the sections with their word shares, so the plan is a budget and the ending keeps its room.
Credit the effect each section is named for, and the ending that resolves what the opening raised — the plan’s words should show the structure, purpose and effect the piece is for.
The model plan is the standard: four steps, sections marked, shares given, ending kept.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Plan a Section B-style review task of 600–900 words: a website review of a one-day first-aid course you attended, judged against criteria the review sets. Set out the shape, the sections with their word shares, the effect each section is for, and the ending. The model plan is the answer.
items.canonical_answer:
Shape: a review’s judgement — introduction, account, evaluation by criteria, verdict — for a website review of a one-day first-aid course.
Sections and shares (750 words total):
1. Introduction — 90 words. What the course is, who I am (a parent with no medical background), and the reader it matters to. Effect: the deciding reader recognises themselves.
2. Account — 160 words. What actually happened across the day, told in the order that shows its logic: the morning’s theory, the afternoon’s practice. Effect: the reader can see the course, not just be told about it.
3. Evaluation: teaching — 130 words. Criterion one: was it taught by someone who could teach? The instructor’s method, with two moments quoted. Effect: judgement by evidence, not impression.
4. Evaluation: value — 130 words. Criterion two: was the price worth what it bought? The cost against the alternatives and the outcomes. Effect: the deciding reader’s real question answered.
5. Evaluation: limitations — 100 words. What the course does not do, stated fairly. Effect: credibility — a review that admits limits is believed about strengths.
6. Verdict — 80 words. The judgement, graded and for whom. Effect: the review’s promise kept; the reader leaves able to decide.
Structure notes: criteria set before the evaluation so the reader can check the logic; end on the verdict’s terms, not a restatement of the day.
marking_guidance: Credit the shape: the category’s own form — arc, exploration or judgement — made visible in the sections.
Credit the sections with their word shares, so the plan is a budget and the ending keeps its room.
Credit the effect each section is named for, and the ending that resolves what the opening raised — the plan’s words should show the structure, purpose and effect the piece is for.
The model plan is the standard: four steps, sections marked, shares given, ending kept.

items.prompt: Here are four bare notes on one point: "First-aid course: judged by retention. Certificate easy, retention hard. At sports day I used the nose-positioning drill. Reflexes, not certificates, are the product." Build them into one developed, coherent paragraph. The model paragraph is the answer.
items.canonical_answer:
The four notes, built into a paragraph:
Topic sentence: A first-aid course is judged, in the end, by what you can still do six months later.
Reason: the certificate is easy — the retention is hard, because a day of information decays unless the day was built to survive it.
Example: at the school sports day in September, I stopped a bleeding nose with the positioning the instructor made us practise until it was a reflex — and while I did it, I realised I was counting to thirty, exactly as drilled, without deciding to.
Consequence: the course’s real product is not the certificate on the wall but the reflex under the pressure — which is why a review should ask how the day was taught, not what it covered.
(The paragraph runs claim, reason, example, consequence, and the example is small enough to see: a nose, a count, a September afternoon.)
marking_guidance: Credit the paragraph: a topic sentence that makes a claim, and every note carried into its text, because the building is the skill and the effect is what the paragraph leaves.
Credit the development: reason, example and consequence visible in the words, with the example small enough to see.
Credit the coherence: every sentence serving the topic, so the paragraph is one thing and not four notes in a row.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is an undeveloped paragraph of about 60 words: "The market is worth visiting. There is a lot of fruit. The fruit is fresh and cheap. Many people come from far away to buy it. The market also sells crafts. You can spend a whole morning there." Build it into a developed, coherent paragraph. The model paragraph is the answer.
items.canonical_answer:
The 60-word undeveloped paragraph, built up (model, about 150 words):
The market is worth visiting for the fruit row alone. I say this as someone who came for the crafts and was converted by the tomatoes. The fruit sellers stack in pyramids — the pyramid is a local art, and the sellers will tell you so — and by eight in the morning the colours are doing the work the price tags are not: six kinds of tomato, three of mango, and a pile of guavas that made a grown man next to me say, out loud, that he had forgotten guavas existed. That is the market’s trick. You come for the crafts, and the fruit row reminds you what fruit is supposed to look like, and you leave with a bag you did not plan.
(The development adds what the original lacked: a reason (the pyramids, the colours), examples small enough to see (six tomatoes, the guava man), and a consequence (the bag you did not plan) — the same point, carried.)
marking_guidance: Credit the paragraph: the bare point carried with reason, example and consequence, because the developing is the skill and the effect on the reader is the proof.
Credit the coherence: one topic served by every sentence, with discourse markers showing the relations.
Credit the difference from repetition: the model adds content, not phrasing, so the words show the development.
